title: At the café
goal: Order food and drinks politely with *ik wil graag* and *mag ik*, and get to know Dutch café habits.
bekal: order without sounding rude — the key is the word *graag*
read the most common Dutch café menu
ask for the bill and pay together or separately
wave: Review **Unit 5**: name ten members of your family with the right possessive, then turn each sentence into a question about age.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Op het terras
dialogs.intro: The sun is out for the first time in a week. The whole town, it seems, is sitting outside on a terrace.

lines.speaker: Ober:
lines.id: Good afternoon. What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Voor mij een koffie verkeerd, alstublieft.
lines.id: A milky coffee for me, please.
lines.literal: for me a coffee wrong, please.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: En ik wil graag een thee met citroen.
lines.id: And I'd like a tea with lemon.
lines.literal: and I want gladly a tea with lemon.

lines.speaker: Ober:
lines.text: Wilt u er iets bij eten?
lines.id: Would you like something to eat with that?
lines.literal: want you there something with eat?

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: Let's have a portion of bitterballen.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Gefrituurde balletjes met vlees erin. Heel lekker.
lines.id: Deep-fried little balls with meat inside. Really tasty.
lines.literal: deep-fried little-balls with meat there-in. very tasty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nee, dank u. O wacht — mag ik ook een glaasje water?
lines.id: No, thank you. Oh wait — could I have a glass of water too?
lines.literal: no, thank you. oh wait — may I also a little-glass water?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Kraanwater is prima. Dank u wel.
lines.id: Tap water is fine. Thank you.
lines.literal: tap-water is fine. thank you indeed.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.id: And we'll pay separately later, OK?

notes: **Wat mag het zijn?** — the most common waiter's greeting, literally "what may it be?". Other versions: *Zegt u het maar* and *Wat kan ik voor u doen?*
**Koffie verkeerd** literally means "wrong coffee" — more milk than coffee, roughly a *latte*. The name isn't a joke; that's how the menu says it.

**Ik wil graag …** is the safest way to order ("I'd like …"). Without *graag*, *ik wil een koffie* sounds like an order barked at the waiter ("I want a coffee"). This little word carries all the politeness.
**Doe maar …** = "just bring me … then" — a relaxed, very Dutch way of ordering. *Maar* here isn't "but" but a softener: *doe maar*, *zeg het maar*, *ga maar zitten*.
**Gefrituurde balletjes met vlees erin** — note *erin* (in it, "therein"). The word *er* turns up again; it will keep turning up until you stop noticing it.
**Een glaasje water** — the small form once more. Ordering *een water* sounds odd; the Dutch order *een glaasje water*, *een biertje*, *een kopje thee*.
**Kraanwater** — tap water, free and safe to drink all over the Netherlands, though some cafés add a small charge. Asking for tap water isn't considered stingy at all.

**De rekening apart** — paying separately is the norm, not the exception. English even has an expression for it: *going Dutch*. In the Netherlands people say *ieder betaalt voor zichzelf*, or use the app *Tikkie* to ask a friend for a few euros without the slightest awkwardness.

grammars.title: Ways to order, from most casual to most polite
body: They're all correct. Only the tone is different.

head: Form
Example
Tone
rows: polite, a little like asking permission
short, when the order goes round the table

after: *Graag* has no direct English equivalent — it means "gladly" and sticks to everything: *graag gedaan* (you're welcome), *ja, graag* (yes, please), *ik eet graag rijst* (I like eating rice).
⚠️ *Ik wil* without *graag* sounds rude to Dutch ears. It's one of the most common politeness mistakes beginners make, and one of the easiest to fix.

grammars.title: Mogen and willen — your first two helper verbs
body: Helper (modal) verbs send the main verb to the **end of the sentence** in its dictionary form. All five are covered in Unit 13; the two most useful ones are already in use now.
after: *Ik wil graag een kopje koffie **drinken**.* — the main verb stands right at the back. When the meaning is clear, the main verb can be dropped altogether: *Ik wil graag een kopje koffie.*
⚠️ False friend: *ik wil* means "I want", not "I will". *Mag ik …?* asks permission; *Kan ik …?* asks whether something is possible. Both are used in cafés, but *mag* sounds softer.

blocks.title: Café habits worth knowing in advance
items: **Coffee comes with a little cookie** (*een koekje*) — and it's free. No need to turn it down.
**Borrel** = after-work drinks, usually on Friday, with beer and fried snacks. The invitation goes: *Gaan we borrelen?*
**Terraces** open the moment the sun comes out, even at 12 degrees. Blankets are draped over the chairs.
**Waiters don't keep coming back.** To call one, raise your hand and say *Mag ik afrekenen?* or *De rekening, alstublieft.*
⚠️ In many small cafés you order and **pay at the counter**, not at the table. If in doubt, watch whether other people are standing in line.

blocks.text: *Eet smakelijk* is said before a meal by anyone passing your table — the waiter, the people at the next table, even strangers. The reply is just *dank je* or *jij ook*.

If you avoid pork, *Ik eet geen varkensvlees* works far better than asking whether a dish is halal: pork hides in many Dutch soups and snacks, and the waiter usually knows right away which dishes are safe once you say it.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of willen or mogen.
Build a polite order from these words.

items: I'd like a glass of water.

answers: Ik wil graag een koffie. — Mag ik de kaart? — Voor mij een thee. — Doe maar een portie bitterballen. — De rekening, alstublieft.
Ik wil graag een glaasje water. — Mag ik de kaart? — Het smaakt heerlijk. — Ik eet geen varkensvlees. — Kunnen we apart betalen? — De rekening, alstublieft.
